newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Ex-Merrill banker meets Singapore order to return.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Merrill banker meets Singapore order to return.

text.p: Ex-Merrill Lynch banker Kevin Wallace has applied to the Hong Kong courts and police to return to Singapore for questioning over assets he declared to the courts here, a lawyer close to the case said on Friday.

The Singapore High Court had given Wallace, a 46-year-old American accused of fraud while employed by the U.S. investment bank as a financial consultant, until August 7 to comply with an order to return.
The court ruled last week Wallace had to travel to the island for cross-examination over assets he declared to the court.
"Yes, he has complied with the Singapore order of court," the lawyer told Reuters.
"They have made application to allow him to come to Singapore," he added, noting this was to seek permission from the Hong Kong judiciary and police to travel here.
Asked when permission was likely to be granted, the lawyer said this was up to the police.
Wallace's Hong Kong lawyer could not be reached for comment but is believed to have written to the Justice Department and police asking if they had objections to the planned travel.
But one government prosecutor involved in Wallace's criminal case in Hong Kong said no formal application had been received.
"He's made no formal application in the criminal proceedings, but I do not know what application he may have made in the civil proceedings."
The prosecutor said Wallace's American passport was still impounded, a condition attached to his court bail.
Wallace was charged in Hong Kong with money laundering but was freed on bail of more than HK$1 million.
In June, Merrill Lynch started civil proceedings against Wallace in Singapore and Hong Kong. It also lodged a criminal complaint in Singapore but no charges have yet been brought.
The bank subsequently succeeded in securing several orders against Wallace, including an injunction to freeze US$15 million of his assets worldwide.
Merrill has accused Wallace of unauthorised trading, misrepresenting or falsifying private clients' statements and forging client signatures.
Wallace worked as a financial consultant to wealthy Asian clients while employed by Merrill from late 1991 until he was dismissed on May 15 this year.
In Singapore this week, Wallace lost his appeal against an order which includes his wife's assets in actions against him.
The outcome of Wallace's application in Hong Kong, to have the High Court there discharge a similar injunction against him, is not known. Hearings were concluded on Thursday.
